# World3D river water: flowing rivers

Verified: 2026-11-01 for the drop cloud and air drag on the broken sheet (GG-572: unit tests, the offline Steinsdalsfossen width measure, and page shots), and for the falling sheet's lip direction and break-up length (unit tests, an offline Steinsdalsfossen measure from the warm start, and seven-falls page shots of the Steinsdalsfossen face, side and top and the pool lip); 2026-10-31 for the GG-537 load step (unit tests; the live Sinzheim save is not checked yet), 2026-10-30 for the river's water from the world (GG-534: unit tests and the live reach at Sinzheim) and the one-water follow (step 1: unit tests and a live move at Sinzheim), 2026-10-27 for the sparse live pictures (GG-430: bench hashes, unit tests and a live page check), and 2026-10-26 against the game world on WebGPU, step 5 (the post chain: rig shots under `?gpu=1` before and after, against `?gpu=0`, patch means and a GTAO parameter sweep on the live page; see "Step 5") and steps 3 and 4 (posed shots under `?gpu=1` and `?gpu=0`, patch means, dome rows against the authored math; see "Steps 3 and 4"); 2026-10-24 against the falling sheet, the warm start and the filled basins (seven-falls page shots at 60 s of flow; static captures 0 px changed on 5 poses); 2026-10-21 against the resident GPU session (bit parity with the earlier resident code, GPU-only timing, live A/B), the flow-map worker timing and output hashes, and the picture blend; and, earlier the same day, the in-place startup-capacity repair, actual production GPU stepping, source-volume progression and rendered source/pool. Full seven-fall acceptance remains open.

## Spells, water cost and the game world on WebGPU

Verified: 2026-10-29 (the world's one ground under the river: unit tests, the channel probe and live shots on 17,4); 2026-10-26 (the water layer's slices 1 to 3 and the mirror's plant cost, against the source and rendered A/B frames).

### One water in the game world (Remy, 2026-10-30)

The game world draws two different rivers today. On every river it draws the static sheet (`waterGeometry.ts`, `WaterPiece`): a flat surface at a fixed waterline, colored by the depth under it, with no flow. Under `?gpu=1&riverSite=world` the live river (this document's solver and water layer) replaces the sheet in one 350 m x 140 m box near the spawn, and the box does not move. The two do not agree on the water height: the sheet's waterline stands above the loader's carved bed, and the live river fills only the channel depth over it.

Remy ruled on 2026-10-30 that the live water is the only water (ADR 0009, amendment of 2026-10-30). Order of work:

1. **The live river follows the player.** The reach anchors on the river nearest the player and moves to a new anchor when the player leaves its inner part or another river comes nearer. The new reach starts from the old reach's water where the two boxes overlap (the solver's `field` start) and from the design level elsewhere.
2. **The live water on by default** in the WebGPU world, with no `riverSite` flag.
3. **Every river in view.** More than one reach: the nearest at 0.5 m cells, farther ones on coarser cells of the same solver. No static sheet where a river runs.
4. **Lakes and town channels** from the same solver: a basin fills to its outlet level.
5. **The static sheet removed** (`waterGeometry.ts` water and `WaterPiece`), then the WebGL world removed (ADR 0009 step 7).
6. **The sea** joins by ADR 0006: the ocean surface takes the river reader at the mouth.

The live water's own open faults stay on their own gap rows; Remy noted on 2026-10-30 that "there are still issues with that water in general".

**Step 1 built (2026-10-30, under `?gpu=1&riverSite=world`).**

- `followWorldRiver` in `riverWorldSite.ts` mounts the reach on the river nearest the player's foot. The scene publishes the foot through `worldGroundHook.ts` (`publishWorldPlayer`): the walking avatar's live foot every frame, and the game's stored position only until the avatar walks.
- The reach moves when the foot's point on the river is more than 90 m from the anchor (`FOLLOW_SHIFT_M`; the box runs 175 m each way), when another river is 30 m nearer, or when the ground world changes. It does not move when the player is more than 250 m from every river line.
- The next reach builds hidden (`activate: false`), then the old reach leaves the chain and the cut and the new one enters in the same call.
- The next reach starts from the old reach's water where the boxes overlap. The old solver sends copies of its depth, discharges and bed (`live-export-water`). The new solver keeps the old water SURFACE over its own bed and turns the velocity into its own axes (`carryRiverWater` in `riverWorldBed.ts`, after `startCold`; unit tests in `riverWorldBed.test.ts`). Cells outside the old box keep the design level.
- Probe hook: `window.__wf3dGround.placePlayerFoot(x, z, holdMs)` stands a foot for the follow where the town blocks a long walk, and `window.__wf3dRiverFollow` shows the moves.

Proof at Sinzheim (`?dummy=1&gpu=1&riverSite=world`, the game save): a probe foot 120 m downstream moved the reach 120 m in 2.5 s and carried 128,022 of 196,000 cells. When the hold ended, the reach came back to the player and carried 128,021 cells again. The solver stayed healthy after each move.

Found on the way:

- The game's own WebGPU world drew black; fixed for the world (GG-535).
- The reach runs at the river page's 1.5 m³/s on the 35 m Sinzheim river and drains to a dry channel (GG-534). That is the next step before the live water can be the default.
- The cold part of a moved reach starts at the design level: 3,008 m³ against the old reach's 1,754 m³, settling to 2,844 m³ in 100 s of solver time.
- The game camera started inside a tree canopy, and a long click-to-move from the Sinzheim bridge reports "That direction was blocked".

Seen on 2026-10-30 at 17,4 (`?phase=world3d&ground=1&gpu=1&riverSite=world&gx=17&gy=4`): the reach mounted on the WebGPU backend with the post chain ready, healthy, 16,243 wet cells, 1.5 m³/s in.

**The river's water comes from the world (GG-534, 2026-10-30).** Remy: "the complexity lies in the co-play between landscape and water quantity." One chain in `src/systems/worldforge/region/riverChannel.ts` sets the channel and the water:

1. **Water count.** The atlas adds up rain downhill (FMG `cells.fl`). It grows at each tributary. It is a relative count: read as m³/s, the map's width curve gives slot canyons (the median river 11 m wide and 7 m deep).
2. **Width** at each point, from the count (`riverWidthFt`, the map's own curve). The region bank carries it per centerline point (`RegionRiverBank.widthFtAt`), and so does the ground line (`GroundPolyline.widthAtM`). `widthFt` and `widthM` stay the mouth's.
3. **Normal flow** of that width: w = 7.2 Q^0.5 (Moody and Troutman 2002).
4. **Channel**: the depth at which the flood (3 times the normal flow, a stated input, GG-540) fills a trapezoid with banks at repose (32 degrees), at the river's fall (Manning, n 0.04).
5. **Fall** from the atlas heights along the river's cells, over a window that widens until the water falls, on into the parent river (`slopeAt`).

Readers:

- **Region tier:** the carve depth is the channel depth per point; crossings read the width where they cross; the town reads the width at the town; the local tier, far shells, travel check and 2D map draw the width per point.
- **3D ground:** `carveRiverChannelToGrade` cuts the channel: the flood level is the lower bank, falling at least at the atlas grade; the bed is the flood level less the depth, and the banks rise at repose to one depth past the flood level. In a town the channel keeps the river's own width: the town plan spans its bridges for that width, while the town's 3D water body is capped at 12 m, which cannot pass the river (GG-538). The static waterline stands at the normal depth over the bed (a town keeps its own surface as a floor, GG-538).
- **Live reach:** `worldReachWater` in `riverWorldSite.ts` gives the normal flow at the box's west edge, the channel's normal depth at the anchor (the design level), half the widest cut width, and each tributary whose line ends inside the box near the course. The worker's default shape takes the total flow (`riverReach.ts` `defaultDischargeM3S`); a tributary's mouth cells take its share and move along it (`withWorldTributaries` in `riverLive.ts`). Probe: `window.__wf3dRiverSite.world.water`.

Proof at Sinzheim (2026-10-30, `?dummy=1&gpu=1&riverSite=world`): 24.2 m³/s in (was 1.5), a 2.7 m channel with 1.4 m of normal water; 23.4 m³/s out and about 12,500 m³ steady after 440 s, healthy; the water fills the channel bank to bank under the bridge (shot `.agent/scratch/one-water/sinzheim-world-flow.jpg`). A follow move of 120 m carried 127,825 cells at the same flow. The tributary path is unit-tested (`riverWorldBed.test.ts`); no tributary ends inside the Sinzheim box, so it is not yet seen live.

Found: a save that stood in the old, higher static water loses its footing (GG-537); the town's own surface stands 1.8 m over the river's level (GG-538); near the mouth the river runs in a 10 m slot, not a valley (GG-539); each window grades on its own (GG-536).

Saved feet after a water change (GG-537, fixed 2026-10-31). A save keeps exact feet, so a new water or ground rule can leave them with no support. On load, `groundFootingRecovery.ts` seats such feet once at the nearest place the measured body can stand, and the player reads a notice that says how far they moved. The step waits for the full-detail chunk under the feet and uses the standing check of the legacy save inspection, so it never seats a body in water too deep to wade. Supported saves are never moved, and walking keeps its refusal.

### Spells reshape the river's ground (2026-10-25)

- `riverSpells.ts` turns four spells into exact terrain-brush shapes (the brush's new `shape` command: hole, trench, wall): Mold Earth digs a 5 ft hole, Move Earth cuts a channel up to 40 ft long, Wall of Stone raises a dam up to 100 ft long with a level crest, Disintegrate cuts a 10 ft notch. The river page casts them from the Terrain tab, and `__RIVER__.live.castSpell` casts them from code.
- A brush or spell edit now keeps the water's volume (`RiverFlowSolver.updateBed` `keepVolume`): each cell keeps its depth and momentum while its ground moves, and the solver moves the water from there. Course and shape edits keep the surface, as before. Every spell shows 0.000 m³ made or lost.
- `riverSpells.test.ts`: a hole dug 11 m from the river and joined by a channel fills to the river's level; a dam ponds the water above and starves the river below; a breach floods the reach below within 25 s.

### The world's one ground under the river (GG-533, 2026-10-29)

Remy, 2026-10-29: the water must react to the land shape, spells change the land, and the world must hold one real ground that the water stands on. Every land shape comes from generator logic, never from hand-drawn terrain.

- **The ground record** (`src/systems/worldforge/bridge/groundRecord.ts`) is the ground world's own height grid (1.524 m) after generation and every carve, plus the ordered list of ground edits. An edit is a `shape-ground` world delta (`delta/types.ts`), so it saves with the player's other world changes and replays on the next build (`makeGroundWorld`, after the carves). A live edit (`editGround`) changes the grid in place and tells every listener the box it changed.
- **One shape math.** The hole, trench and wall of `riverSpells.ts` moved to `terrain/groundShapeProfile.ts`. The river's brush and the ground record both call it, so one spell cuts one shape everywhere.
- **The river's bed reads the record.** Inside its corridor (the strip where the world's terrain is cut) the bed is the fine grid, not the drawn 8 m lattice; it eases to the lattice over 3 m and is the lattice for the last 1 m before the cut line, so it still meets the drawn ground (`riverWorldBed.ts` `RiverBedCorridor`). On 17,4 the lattice had made a chain of diamond pools: the floor's width swung from 9.5 m to 1 m every 24 m. On the fine grid it holds 10.5 to 12.5 m over the probed 50 m, and the wet area rose from 8,794 to 16,333 cells (`.agent/scratch/water-campaign/diamondprobe.mjs`).
- **A live edit reaches the water.** The river site hears each edit, reads the new fine values over its box and sends them to the solver (`live-world-ground`). The solver rebuilds its bed there and keeps the water's volume, as for a spell on the river page; the drawn bed takes the returned patch. A wall cut across the channel at river-local x = 60 came back in 76 ms, and the water backed up behind it on screen.
- **Probe hook:** `window.__wf3dGround.edit({ shape, x, z, x2, z2, radius, depth })` in ground meters (`toGround` turns a scene point into them).
- **Readers of a live edit:** the drawn terrain and its roads take every edit too (2026-10-29; see `streamed-3d-world.md`, "Ground edits on the drawn ground"). Not yet: a volume bubble already built (a bubble built after an edit has it), and the trees, props, buildings and static water over an edit. Game spells reach it too (GG-533 step 3, 2026-10-29): a spell that moves earth in a world-sourced fight cuts its shape through `editGround` and saves it; see `combat.md`, "Spells that move earth reach the world's ground". A blast digs a `crater` shape, the 3D arena's sphere cut.
- **Seen in the shots, not fixed here:** the fine grid shows the town channel's true carve, a near-vertical wall about 4 m high, whose bank texture stretches; a tree stands in the channel. Both are generator rules to fix (GG-533).

### The water's frame cost (2026-10-26)

Default river page, 2560 x 1440, vsync off (`.agent/scratch/water-campaign/perfwater.mjs`, `perfmirror.mjs`). The water's budget is a quarter of the 16.7 ms frame, 4.2 ms.

| View | Water surface (GPU) | Mirror pass (GPU) | Water total | Whole frame |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Wide (river-system) | 2.6 ms | 4.2 ms (3.4 ms at 1 sample) | 6.8 ms, over | 25.4 ms |
| Bank (bank-along) | 1.7 ms | 2.3 ms (1.7 ms at 1 sample) | 4.0 ms | 12.3 ms |

The mirror draws the whole scene again at half size (9.6 million triangles in the wide view), so its cost follows the scene's geometry, not the water. The next cut is to draw less into the mirror. The wide view also misses 60 fps without water: its main pass draws 9.4 million triangles in 17.1 ms.

### Game world on WebGPU (ADR 0009, 2026-10-26)

Inventory of the game world's WebGL-only parts (read-only scout):

- R3F 9.5 accepts an async WebGPURenderer through the Canvas `gl` factory; `WebGPUProbeScene.tsx` and `BattleMap3DGpuScene.tsx` (`?gpu=1`) already use that pattern, and reject a silent WebGL2 fallback.
- 18 sites in the world's render path fail under WebGPU (13 shaders or effects): terrain surface noise and the substance ground (`onBeforeCompile`, silent loss), the world water tint, grass wind sway and tree foliage tint (`onBeforeCompile`), the gradient sky and moon (`ShaderMaterial`), takram Sky, Stars and Clouds (WebGL libraries), the toon rim, outline and blob shadow (`toon.ts`), and the EffectComposer chain (N8AO, ACES tone mapping, SMAA).
- About 46 sites are plain built-in materials that convert by themselves, if R3F lights reach the node lights at r172 (three #30044 broke this on r170: check it first).
- The r172 faults apply: linear fog drawn twice, hemisphere light space, per-camera shadows, instanced count fixed at first draw, late-mounted lights.
- Shared factories (`substanceGroundMaterial`, `waterSurfaceMaterial`, `toon.ts`) have WebGL users on other pages; each keeps a WebGL version or gets a recorded gap.
- The river view owns its renderer, canvas and four passes (reflection, opaque color and depth, water, output). To mount in the world it needs a mode that takes the world's renderer, scene and camera, and the world must render an opaque color and depth pass first.

Order of work:
1. Renderer swap behind a URL flag, built-in materials only; shared hemisphere-light node; composer off; check lights, fog, shadows and instance counts.
2. Characters through `swapEntityMaterialsForGpu`.
3. Gradient sky and moon to TSL.
4. Terrain noise, substance ground, world water tint, grass wind, tree tint to TSL node materials (pattern: `BattleMap/gpu/terrainColorNode.ts`).
5. Post chain to three's node `PostProcessing` (scene pass with depth, GTAO, ACES, SMAA).
6. The live river in the world: a `RiverReachView` mode on the world's renderer; then the frame budget. (Built as the water layer, below.)
7. Clouds and takram sky (a three upgrade or own TSL), WebGPU default, delete the WebGL path.

#### Steps 3 and 4: the world's GLSL looks as TSL node materials (2026-10-26)

Each WebGL shader stays in place for `?gpu=0`. Under `?gpu=1` the scene mounts a TSL twin from `src/components/World3D/gpu/`. Each twin reproduces the GLSL math; the constants are imported from the WebGL module where the GLSL had them.

- Gradient sky dome (`gpu/worldGpuSky.ts`, mounted by `World3DLighting.tsx`). The `NodeMaterial: Material "ShaderMaterial" is not compatible` error is gone (22 console messages before, 21 after, rig `world3d.mjs`). The dome's rows match the authored math through ACES at exposure 1.05 within 6 of 255 at every elevation (measured against expected, sRGB: 24 deg 145,148,184 against 139,144,182; 11 deg 171,166,187 against 168,164,187; 1 deg 204,194,196 against 196,187,193). The WebGL frame cannot serve as the reference: in ground mode the volumetric cloud effect covers its sky.
- Moon (`gpu/worldGpuSky.ts`, mounted by `sky/TakramSkySystem.tsx`). Under the flag the component mounts only the moon; takram `<Sky>` and `<Stars>` are WebGL libraries and stay off. The material builds and compiles without an error; it is NOT proven in a render, because the ground camera does not pitch up to the moon (at 23:00 the moon stands 38 deg high; the camera holds a 3 deg pitch).
- Terrain surface noise (`gpu/terrainSurfaceNoiseNode.ts`, `TerrainPiece` and `FrontierSkirt` in `World3DScene.tsx`). Open terrain patches carry the same texture statistics on both renderers (standard deviation per channel 23.4/18.5/12.5 on WebGL against 23.4/18.5/12.4 on WebGPU, town wide shot) and means within 3 to 7 of 255.
- Substance ground (`gpu/substanceGroundNode.ts`, `VolumeGroundBubble.tsx`). The plaza draws the strata, cells, chips and AO instead of flat white. Open patches match (98,80,62 against 98,79,59; 52,44,38 against 54,44,36). Patches next to walls and under the player differ by 20 to 30 of 255: that is N8AO, which is off on WebGPU until step 5.
- World water tint (`gpu/waterSurfaceNode.ts`, `WaterPiece`). Deep water 41,63,89 against 44,68,97 and 7,33,60 against 10,42,73 at the river window (`gx=17&gy=4`); the shallow ramp and the emissive fade show on both.
- Grass wind (`gpu/grassWindNode.ts`, `GrassLayer.tsx`). The sway runs in blade-local space before the instance transform, as the GLSL does, through a `setupPosition` override. Two frames 0.7 s apart differ by 2,018 px on WebGPU and 2,566 px on WebGL at the same pose; the tufts are green on both (60,66,50 against 92,95,78).
- Tree foliage tint (`gpu/treeTintNode.ts`, `VegetationTreeField.tsx`). Bark is brown again (trunk band 52,48,28 WebGL, 70,62,40 WebGPU; 39,40,27 before the port) and leaves keep the biome tint.
- Frame rate: 56 to 60 fps at 1600 x 900 on both renderers in the town; 60 fps at the river window.

#### Step 5: the post chain on WebGPU (2026-10-26)

Under `?gpu=1` in the ground profile, `WorldGpuPostChain` (`World3DScene.tsx`) drives three's node `PostProcessing` from R3F: a `useFrame` at priority 1 makes R3F skip its own render, and the chain draws the frame. The chain is built by `gpu/worldGpuPost.ts`:

```
scenePass = pass(scene, camera, { samples: 0 })        linear half-float color + depth, no MSAA (as the WebGL chain's multisampling 0)
aoFactor  = denoise(ao(depth, normals-from-depth, camera))   GTAO at half size, radius 7 m, depth range 1.5 m, pow 5, 16 samples
lit       = sceneColor * aoFactor
out       = renderOutput(lit)                            ACES at the renderer's exposure 1.05, then sRGB, once
output    = smaa(out)                                     on the final image; postProcessing.outputColorTransform = false
```

`PostProcessing` turns the renderer's tone mapping and output color space off while the passes draw, so the scene pass is linear and `renderOutput` applies both once. The WebGL chain's ToneMapping effect also runs ACES at the renderer's exposure (three's `tonemapping_pars_fragment` multiplies by `toneMappingExposure`, which the renderer sets on every program). The WebGL path (`?gpu=0`) is unchanged: the new component mounts only under the flag. The display addons (GTAO, Denoise, SMAA with its inline textures) load on demand inside `buildWorldGpuPost`, so the WebGL bundle does not carry them.

THE HANDLE FOR THE WATER PASS (step 6). `getWorldGpuPost()` returns the live chain or null; `onWorldGpuPost(listener)` fires on mount and unmount. The handle carries `renderer`, `scene`, `camera`, `post`, `scenePass`, `sceneColor` (`scenePass.getTextureNode('output')`, linear), `sceneDepth` (`scenePass.getTextureNode('depth')`), `aoFactor`, `ao` (the GTAO node and its uniforms) and `setComposite(fn)`: `fn(lit, { sceneColor, sceneDepth, aoFactor })` returns the node the tone mapper reads, so the water layer inserts its water over `lit` after the opaque scene; `setComposite(null)` restores `sceneColor * aoFactor`. The page exposes the handle as `window.__wf3dPost` and its state as `window.__wf3dPostChain` (`building`, `ready`, `failed`). The rigs use `setComposite((lit, p) => p.sceneColor)` for an AO-off frame.

THE AO SETTINGS WERE MEASURED, NOT COPIED. N8AO's values (radius 7 m, `distanceFalloff` 3.5, `intensity` 3.2, half size) were the start. A sweep on the live page (`.agent/scratch/water-campaign/s5sweep.mjs`, 9 then 11 settings at the plaza pose 9 m above the player, then 7 at the river wide view) against the WebGL frame at the same poses gave:

| Patch (sRGB luma) | WebGL (N8AO) | WebGPU no AO | GTAO as N8AO (range 3.5, pow 3.2) | GTAO chosen (range 1.5, pow 5) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Plaza pose, open ground | 55 | 54 | 54 | 54 |
| Plaza pose, tiled roof 4 m from the camera | 27 | 28 | 7 | 28 |
| Plaza pose, foot of a post | 42 | 57 | 44 | 44 |
| River wide, open plaza | 93 | 94 | 94 | 94 |
| River wide, foot of a tree | 34 | 64 | 43 | 51 |
| River wide, forest floor | 63 | 75 | 73 | 74 |

GTAO's `thickness` is a hard depth cut where N8AO's range is a soft weight: at 2 m and above the roof's tile ridges occlude each other (28 -> 6 at 2 m); at 1.5 m the roof holds and `pow 5` brings the post's foot to N8AO's value. Open ground did not move at any setting. Mean scene luma: river wide view WebGPU 77.2 -> 75.1, plaza wide view 79.4 -> 76.7 (WebGL 57.8 at both; the sky patch alone is 182 against 38).

Frame rate at 1600 x 900 (headless Chrome, rig perf snapshots, vsync bucketed): town plaza WebGL 53.9 fps, WebGPU 47.0 before and 41.1, 49.8, 59.9 and 60.0 after (four valid runs; the headless host's snapshot is noisy on this heavier scene); river window WebGL 60.0, WebGPU 60.0 before and 59.9 after.

Shots (gitignored): `.agent/scratch/water-campaign/shots/world3d/s5b-*` (before, both renderers), `s5f-gpu-river-*`, `s5f2-gpu-plaza-*` (after), `sw*-plaza-*` and `sw3-river-*` (the sweep frames), measured with `s5measure.mjs`.

Open gaps (step 5):

- GG: wide creases. N8AO darkens a tree foot to 34 and the forest floor to 63 where GTAO with the 1.5 m range reaches 51 and 74. Candidates: true normals through MRT (`scenePass.setMRT({ output, normal })`) so the range can widen without the roof artifact, or a depth-aware soft range in place of the hard cut.
- GG: one rig run drew a black canvas (page background only, no console error, 54 fps reported) on the first page load after a source edit of `worldGpuPost.ts`; three later loads and a second record run drew normally. Not reproduced; the rigs now read `__wf3dPostChain`.
- GG: the first load after a new addon import failed with Vite's `504 Outdated Optimize Dep` (the chain logged `failed` and the world drew plain); the second load worked. Known Vite lazy-dep wedge, not a code fault.
- GG: no clouds (step 7). The continent profile has no post chain on either renderer, as before.

### The mirror's plant cost (2026-10-26)

The plants cause most of the mirror's cost. Each object group was hidden from the mirror only, and the frame timed (live page, 2560 x 1440, vsync off, `.agent/scratch/water-campaign/mirrorgroups.mjs`):

| Group hidden from the mirror | Wide view saved | Bank view saved |
|---|---|---|
| Tree leaf cards | 0.94 to 0.98 ms | 0.43 ms |
| Bush and shrub leaf cards | 0.54 to 0.57 ms | 0.20 ms |
| Tree wood (trunks and branches) | 0.33 to 0.35 ms | 0.02 ms |
| Bush wood | 0.33 ms | 0.00 ms |
| Ground tiles | 0.11 ms | 0.00 ms |

Two cuts that change no pixel are on in the live page (`liveWanted()`). A static capture keeps the shipped mirror, so the reference shots stay pixel-identical.

- THE WATER MASK (`riverMirrorMask.ts`). The water reads the mirror at the projection of a point 18 m along its reflected ray, turned by the ripples and, for rough water, read again along the ray turned up by 0.5. The mask marks, on a 96 x 54 screen grid, every cell that such a read from a wet cell can reach (an 8 m ripple reach at the read: a slope of 0.2). The plant cull draws a mirror plant only when its mirror image meets a marked cell. It cut the wide view's mirror triangles by 19 % and moved no scene pixel on six views.
- THE STAND-IN BRANCHES (`riverVegetation.ts` `liteBranches`). The far trees' mirror copies keep the largest 40 % of their limb tubes, the same triangles on the same vertex buffers, so no limb bends differently. The wide view's full-detail mirror branches fell from 3.4 M to 0.17 M triangles; at most 0.003 % of pixels moved.
- Together they save 0.2 to 0.5 ms. The leaf cards, not the triangles, carry most of the plant cost.

A smaller mirror (a third of the frame, or one MSAA sample) saves 1 to 1.5 ms more, but on calm water (calm-bridge) the reflected leaves turn blocky and lose their sky gaps: about 3 % of pixels move. The live page therefore keeps the half-size 4x mirror; `&mirror=lite` asks for the small one. (WebGPU allows 1 or 4 samples; 2 breaks the mirror.) The rest of the budget is GG-525.

The live river's water is moving out of `RiverReachView` into parts the game world can draw too: one water system. ## Detected fall lips

### The airborne spill finds every lip from the bed and the water (2026-10-21)

The live seven-falls course (`riverCourse=references`) now launches water into the airborne spill at every fall lip. No hand list chooses the lips. Remy's complaint on 2026-10-21 was a film down the raised pool's wall: "this is not how water flows from a waterfall".

How it works now:

- `RiverSpillTransfer` has a `detect` mode (`src/systems/world3d/river/riverSpillTransfer.ts`). `LiveRiver` builds it in that mode. The old hand list near `POOL_SPILL.crestS` (`refreshSpillFaces`) is removed.
- Each step, every native face with outgoing water takes the SEPARATION TEST. Read the bed as straight between cell centers. The donor water moves at its normal speed un along the slope S it came down (S = 0 when the cell behind it is dry). A free jet falls S·d + ½·g·τ² across the gap d, with τ = d·√(1+S²)/un. The water leaves the bed when the bed falls further than that. On a straight slope the water stays on the bed, as on a spillway face.
- The bed drop must also exceed the flow depth, and the receiving surface must stand below the lip bed.
- The release velocity turns the solver speed down the slope and keeps its size. The kinematic form w = u·tan θ gave −374 m/s on the Seven Sisters face, five times the free-fall speed of the whole drop.
- One face merges its releases over at most 0.1 s into one parcel (`mergeWindowS`). Volume and momentum add exactly; the gravity impulse takes the age change. A Top up transient made 82,000 parcels in 0.3 s of flow before the merge, and 9,800 after it.
- `RiverScene.tsx` turns the spill on by default for the live seven-falls course. `spill=0` turns it off. `spill=1` still turns it on for the other headwaters courses. Captures stay static, because the headwaters are off without `live`.

Proof (rigs and shots in `.agent/scratch/fall-lips/`, gitignored):

- 24 unit tests pass in `src/systems/world3d/river/__tests__/riverSpillTransfer.test.ts`, 9 of them new for the detect mode.
- A headless dry start on the full course launches at the pool lip from 2,448 s of flow, then at Storfossen, Seven Sisters, Steinsdalsfossen, Latefossen, Tvindefossen and Stigfossen. At 4,274 s: 12,607 m³ launched, 12,586 m³ landed, 4,274 parcels in flight, volume error −7.8e-10 m³.
- Before and after page shots at the same poses and 3,401 s of flow (`shots/before-after-sheet.png`): both pages healthy with 0 restores, 5,096.6 m³ against 5,096.1 m³ of water, 56 to 60 fps.

### The falling sheet, the warm start and the filled basins (2026-10-24)

- THE FALLING SHEET. `RiverSpillView` draws each lip face's parcels as one connected ribbon from the lip to the landing (`spillNappeStations`, `buildSpillNappeGeometry`, `spillNappeMaterial`), by default; `useSheet(false)` gives the prisms. Thickness is q / speed, the width spreads by `JET_SPREAD`, and the white share follows `breakupLengthM` and `jetWhiteness` (`waterfallTypes.ts`). Steinsdalsfossen now falls as a white curtain into its pool.
- THE SHEET'S LIP AND BREAK-UP (2026-11-01). Two measured faults kept the Steinsdalsfossen curtain straight and white from the lip (offline run from the warm start, `.agent/scratch/fall-lips/steins.mts`):
  - Each ribbon spread along its own grid face. Its lip is a diagonal stair of 39 x and z faces, so once the water turned down, 27 of the 39 ribbons stood edge-on to the front view, and the spread went into depth. Now each station's span lies along the lip: horizontal and square to the launch flow. Each face's width is projected onto that line, so the faces add up to the lip's true 14 m, and q (thickness) rises to match. The drawn span keeps the full face width: exact tiling showed the rock through V-shaped gaps at the pool lip, because the stair's faces sit at different depths along the flow.
  - `breakupLengthM` had dropped the Fr^2 and turbulence terms of Ervine, Falvey and Withers, and gave 0.06 to 0.12 m. The full law, with Castillo's 1.2 % lip turbulence (`LIP_TURBULENCE`), gives 1.9 to 4.1 m there. Horeni's nappe formula, 6 q^0.32, agrees within 11 %.
  - Result: seen from the front, the curtain widens from 9.3 m to 10.9 m over its 50 m (before: 9.0 to 10.1 m), and its top 2 to 4 m stay clear. The reference widens about 2.5 times. Most of that is spray, and the clip's 12 m^3/s; the course's lip carries 1.16 m^3/s. The turbulent spread law (3.8 % per side) is unchanged.
- THE DROP CLOUD AND AIR DRAG (2026-11-01, GG-572). Past its break-up length the sheet is drops in the air it drags, and both the flight and the drawing now say so. The laws are the ocean splash's own (`oceanSplashLaws.ts`), so the falls and the sea use one water; `brokenJetCloud`, `brokenJetDrag` and `dropCloudOpticalDepth` are in `waterfallTypes.ts`:
  - The air. A dense spray drags its own air (two-way coupling: Faeth 1987; Marble 1970). The water's mass loading over the cloud's depth sets the air's share of the water's speed (`splashCoupledShare`), and the drag acts on the slip only (Schiller and Naumann). Just past break-up the water outweighs its air hundreds of times and falls as one body. Lower down the cloud is deep, and the drops slow toward their terminal speed. The drops end at the stable drop, 5.4 mm, and at `splashCoupledStableDrop` in a dense spray.
  - The flight. `RiverSpillTransfer.advance` moves each parcel in substeps (at most 0.01 s or a fifth of a cell), each on the exact parabola of its start acceleration. Before break-up that is gravity alone, so the old free flight is unchanged. A parcel records its `breakAge`. The receipt carries `airDragImpulse`, and the momentum ledger closes with it. A parcel that is a drop cloud takes no more merged water. `airDrag: false` keeps the free flight, for a comparison only.
  - The spread. The jet's air is a turbulent jet, and its eddies carry the drops sideways (Taylor dispersion, `splashTurbulentSigma`: the plane jet's spread 0.10, Pope 2000; the drop's inertia, Hinze 1975). Before break-up the sheet spreads by its own turbulence only: Ervine and Falvey's eq. 1, delta/X = 0.38 Tu, 0.46 % per side at the lip's Tu (`coherentSpreadRate`). `JET_SPREAD` (3.8 %) is that law at Tu = 10 %; the spill sheet no longer uses it, and the headwaters fall still does.
  - The drawing. Each ribbon has four edges (outer, inner, inner, outer, 2 sigma outside and inside its span) and carries its own face's water column at each, a Gaussian blur of the face's flow, so overlapped ribbons add up to the lip's true flow. Past break-up the opacity is the cloud's, 1 - exp(-tau) with tau = (3/2) Q_ext L / D. The shared noise modulates tau about its mean only. Between snapshots the view moves each parcel by its own `acceleration`.
  - Result at Steinsdalsfossen (offline, warm start, 30 s; `.agent/scratch/fall-lips/steins3.mts`, front view): the bottom of the fall moves at 21.8 m/s, against 31.3 m/s in free fall. The drops spread to an rms offset of 2.6 m at 50 to 60 m down. The faint edge (10 % opacity) widens from 9.3 m to 13.8 m; the old hard edges went from 9.4 m to 11.0 m. The dense body (50 % opacity) stays about 9 m wide, and its peak opacity is 0.95 to 0.96. So the published drop laws give this lip a soft fringe, not the clip's wide plume; the flow (1.16 against about 12 m^3/s) is the open question in GG-572.
- Two drawing faults were found and fixed. A face-on sheet made `pow(1 − facing, 5)` NaN, and the page's auto exposure turned one NaN pixel into a black frame. A growing sheet put larger arrays on a geometry the WebGPU renderer had already drawn, and new indices read old vertex data: long thin lines crossed the views and most of the sheet did not show. Growth now makes a new geometry.
- A WALL HIT. A parcel that crosses sideways into a cell whose surface stands above it struck the side of a step. It now lands in the cell before the wall, at that cell's surface. Before, it landed 9 m up the Latefossen staircase.
- FILLED BASINS (GG-427). `spillLevels` (a priority flood from the east edge) gives each cell the level at which water at rest spills; `LiveRiver.fillBasinsToSpill` fills every channel cell to it. On this course Top up uses it and works on the default dry start. The page starts with full basins by default (19,289 m³, 2.2 s); `riverStart=dry` keeps the empty start.
- THE WARM START. `scripts/river/bakeSevenFallsWarmStart.mts` runs the filled start to steady flow and writes `public/data/river/seven-falls-warm.bin` (gitignored, about 2.5 MB). The page loads it (`LiveRiver.startWarm`) if its grid and bed checksum match; the panel line "River start" says which start ran and why. The browser and Node round the terrain math a few last bits apart (about 1e-13 m), so the checksum check allows a gap under 0.001. Page open to falls running: about 3 minutes, against 25 to 30 from dry. Bake again after any course change.
- THE FILM RULE (`uFilmOnSurface`, tune `film`): depth read as h · cos θ. It is OFF everywhere. On the static captures it moved up to 71 pixels a pose; on the live page it brought back NaN black frames at the pool and did not remove the Steinsdalsfossen bars (the bars were the sheet's buffer fault above).

What is still wrong (open):

- The pool lip and Seven Sisters still read mostly as film on rock: their faces are not vertical, so the jets land again within meters (see below). The falling sheet has no landing churn or mist yet (the headwaters fall's `mistRatePerS` law is the candidate).
- On a face that is not vertical, the slow jet lands on the rock again and slides as a film. On the raised pool's 69° face at 1.38 m/s the jet touches the face about 4 m down. This is real behavior for this rock and flow; the rock is not changed by hand (Remy, 2026-10-09).
- The GPU resident path carries the spill since 2026-10-22 (GG-429, the GPU session's `release()` replay).
- The flow-map ripple is still projected in world xz, so a film on a steep face still stretches into streaks.

## Threaded water and FPS work

### Live river: resident GPU session, smooth pictures (2026-10-21)

**The resident GPU path keeps the water on the device.** `RiverGpuResident` (`riverGpuResident.ts`) makes its buffers once for each grid. A request uploads only CPU changes: every cell once (and after a restore, a top-up or any failed interval), whole rows after a bed edit, and single cells for inlet changes. Each interval reads back only the cells the device changed (water, reach flags and time integrals), through a "collect" pass in a second shader module. The CPU copy (`RiverFlowSolver.h/hu/hv/reach`) therefore equals the device water after each interval, so edits, health checks, restores and the synchronized fallback act on the same state as before.

**The device topology is sparse.** `wake` visits only the awake cells and their four neighbors; each cell has one owner thread, so the result does not depend on thread order. `build`, `rows`, `prefix` and `compact` run only in a step where a reach bit changed, and only for the rows next to that change. The per-cell stages use indirect dispatch, and `advance` and `reduce` are one stage (`advanceReduce`).

**Proof.** The old per-interval code and the new session gave the same bits over 12 intervals (48 steps) with a moving wet front: state, integrals, reach and transient flags, clocks, volumes and journals (rig `.agent/scratch/river-pace/gpuparity-run.mjs`). On the GPU alone (no renderer), 4 steps on the 5.9 million-cell grid fell from 147 ms to 18.6 ms. The CPU vs GPU depth gap (0.000181616 m against the 0.0001 m gate) is unchanged by this work: the device arithmetic is the same.

**Live result: the GPU path does not yet win.** At steady flow (about 4,800 awake cells), resident GPU ran 0.63x real time at 19.4 fps; the CPU worker ran 1.00x at 23.9 fps with worker busy 0.55. That GPU run shared the GPU with another 3D page, so its frame rate is not clean. The page is GPU-bound (about 42 ms per frame, 19 ms of it CPU), and the resident exchange waits behind the renderer's frames in one GPU queue (about 240 ms per exchange). The CPU worker stays the default. With the airborne spill on (the default on `riverCourse=references` since 2026-10-21), the resident path fell back to synchronized per-step GPU steps (0.067x); GG-429 below removed that fallback.

**The airborne spill runs inside the resident interval (GG-429, 2026-10-22).** A spill stage on the device runs every gate of `RiverSpillTransfer.launch` in detect mode after the face fluxes; a launched face gives its receiving cell only its bed correction, as `riverSolver.step` does. The device writes a launch list (face, fluxes, donor depth, velocity and slope). After the interval, `RiverFlowSolver.replaySpill` replays it step by step: `beginStep`, that step's `release` calls in native face order with that step's own time and dt, then `advance(time + dt)`. Landed water joins the CPU copy and reaches the device as a cell patch before the next interval, so it enters the device water up to one interval (at most 8 steps, 0.2 s) later than on the CPU path. `release` is the old body of `launch` after its tests, unchanged. A device step equal to the Float32 longest step is replayed as the exact longest step, so the 0.1 s merge window matches the CPU path. Tests: `riverSpillReplay.test.ts` (CPU path and replay give the same parcels and receipts). Bench on a 6 m drop over 30 s: released 3.310091 m3 (CPU 3.310093), returned 2.727949 m3 (CPU 2.727951), spill ledger errors near 1e-15. Live, spill on, one page, free GPU, past 600 s: GPU resident 0.995x real time, worker busy 0.33, 59.0 fps, 4 steps per exchange (46 ms); CPU worker 1.004x, busy 0.37, 59.8 fps. In fast mode the CPU runs 10.5x and the GPU 3.18x, so the CPU worker stays the default. No lip spilled in that window (0 launches): from a dry start the pool lip spills only after about 2,450 s. With live launches (past 2,600 s, the pool lip spills, 3 to 25 launches per exchange) the GPU path leads: GPU resident 1.0008x real time, worker busy 0.34, 58.5 fps, fast 2.76x; CPU worker 0.998x, busy 0.75, 59.0 fps, fast 1.79x. From a dry start the CPU still reaches 2,600 s of flow sooner (309 s against 858 s). The default stays the CPU worker until Remy rules.

**The resident path stalled on the warm start (fixed 2026-10-27).** On the warm start the solver stopped after a few seconds of flow with "Resident GPU validation failed: Invalid BindGroup bindGroup_object". Two faults made this:

- `LandingSprayView` (`riverLandingSpray.ts`) built its InstancedMesh at count 0 with 4,000 slots. three r172 then reads the matrices from a uniform array sized by the whole array (256,000 bytes, over the 65,536-byte limit), so the spray's bind group failed on every frame and the spray did not draw. The mesh now keeps its count at the capacity and draws the live puffs through `InstancedBufferGeometry.instanceCount`.
- `RiverGpuResident.run` kept its validation error scope open across the read-back wait, so it also caught the renderer's errors on the shared device. It now pops the scope right after its submit; the overflow re-copy has its own scope.

Clean A/B on the warm start, past 600 s of flow, one page (rig `measure.mjs`, 2026-10-27):

| | GPU resident | CPU worker |
|---|---|---|
| Real-time mode | 1.004x | 0.24x |
| Fast mode | 1.55x | 0.25x |
| Frame rate | 46 fps | 46 fps |
| Awake cells | 267,000 to 280,000 | about 230,000 |

The CPU worker cannot keep real time on the page's default start; the GPU path can. The earlier A/B figures in this section came from a dry start. With the larger wet area the flow mapper took 2.5 to 3.0 s a picture live (GG-430).

**Longer resident intervals in fast mode (2026-10-27).** An interval holds up to `RIVER_RESIDENT_MAX_STEPS` (32) steps; the source buffer's tail holds 8 control vec4s and 2 journal vec4s for each step (`RIVER_RESIDENT_TAIL`). `residentSlots` asks for the steps at the first step's time step plus two, so unused slots are not dispatched. With no flow-time budget (fast mode) an interval may run 0.8 s of flow (`RIVER_RESIDENT_INTERVAL_S`); real-time mode keeps 0.2 s. Remy approved the less frequent inflow refresh this gives. Warm start, past 600 s: fast mode 2.22 to 2.28x (was 1.55x), 26 to 27 steps for each exchange, warm-up to 600 s of flow in 279 to 289 s (was 419 s). The GPU parity rig still gives the same bits over 12 intervals. Chunked submits with `onSubmittedWorkDone` between chunks let frames in, but each wait cost about 20 ms, so they were not kept.

**Where a resident step's time goes (2026-10-27, rig `gpustage.ts`).** On the GPU alone, with about 290,000 awake cells, a step costs 5.4 to 6.9 ms, and each exchange adds a fixed 11 to 13 ms (read-back and mapping). On the live page the same step cost about 22 ms, so the renderer's share of the one GPU queue (GG-431) is most of the live cost. The bare-GPU numbers show no large write cost in `advanceReduce`. Single-stage timings from that rig are not reliable: a stage run alone can return early at its guards.

**Retarded source changes no longer synchronize.** A resident interval now ends before the first step that would start at or after the next released source change. This replaced a per-step synchronized fallback that copied the whole grid each step (free RAM fell to 0.14 GB at a dry start). Test: `riverResidentSource.test.ts`.

**Worker busy share excludes device wait.** `RiverWorkMeter` reports `waitMs` apart from `busyMs`. In resident mode the worker builds the field frame while the device runs the interval.

**The choppy look came from the flow mapper, not the solver.** The page got a new water picture about every 0.8 to 1.3 s, because the flow-map worker (`LiveFlowMapper.map` / `flowMapCore`) took 720 to 1,430 ms for each picture. It wrote three whole-grid textures, their Float16 copies and a whole-grid level field for about 4,300 wet cells.

**Sparse pictures (GG-430, 2026-10-22 to 2026-10-27).** The mapper now touches only the cells near the water, and the page receives only the changed rows. All output stays bit-identical to the whole-grid mapper (rig `.agent/scratch/river-pace/mapbench.mts`: frame, output and state hashes equal over six pictures). In the dry-start bench (about 4,300 wet cells) a picture after the first takes 84 to 134 ms, from 750 to 1,350 ms. The parts:

- `LiveRiver.frame()` lists its wet cells (`LiveFieldFrame.cells`). The mapper (`flowMapCore` with a `FlowMapScratch`) scans only those cells, grows its rings from the wet front, and keeps its arrays between pictures. It resets only the cells that the previous picture wrote.
- Far from the water (past the 8 level rings) the map keeps the level unfilled as `RIVER_FAR_LEVEL` (-30000). Each picture carries the coarse level grid (`coarse`, one value for each 4 x 4 cells) that the old map interpolated into those cells. `riverFarLevelAt` gives the same value as the old fill. The coarse grid's 60 Jacobi sweeps run in their own small functions (`coarseBins`, `coarseJacobi`), with the same sums in the same order: V8 ran the loop about four times slower inside the large `flowMapCore`.
- After the first picture the map worker sends a row patch (`LiveFlowSnapshot.patch`, from `riverPatchRows` and `riverPatchFrom` in `riverFlowPatch.ts`) and empty whole-grid arrays. `RiverLiveClient` writes the patch into its kept arrays (`applyRiverPatch`) and gives consumers the full arrays, the patch, and `surfaceBeforeAt` (the surface that the patch replaced, for the blend).
- `RiverWaterLayer.updateFlowTextures` uploads a patch picture's rows as a few rectangles (`riverPatchRects`, `updateRiverFlowTexturePatch`). A texture that does not yet hold the kept arrays gets a full upload. It writes the coarse grid into a small half-float texture (`riverCoarseLevelTexture.ts`).
- The bank material reads the level with four texel loads and puts the coarse level in place of each far texel (`createRiverBankMaterial(..., coarse)`). A filtered read would mix -30000 into every texel near a far cell. The CPU samplers (`riverSamplers(d, borrow, coarse)`) do the same.

**On the warm start the mapper cost follows the wet area.** Since 2026-10-24 the page starts from `seven-falls-warm.bin`, with about 151,000 wet cells (the falls run, the pools are full). The sparse mapper then takes about 550 ms a picture at steady state in Node (bench `WARM=1`, 20 maps; 670 ms before the loop moves below), spread over surface 90, sheet 85, pack 75, advection 72, sources 65 and velocity 40 ms. The live page measured 940 to 1,025 ms, one picture every 1.2 to 1.3 s. The October 22 figures (CPU 1.0x real time, about 4,800 awake cells) came from a dry start; on the warm start the CPU solver runs 0.44x in Node and 0.24x on the page (about 230,000 awake cells). V8 note: `flowMapCore` runs its loops through loop-only compiles (OSR) that it drops at the next stage. Moving a loop into a top-level function with parameters cut that loop by up to 4x: `smoothVelocity`, `coarseJacobi`, `coarseBins`, `advectRelaxStep`, `streakStep`, `packCells` and `extendRings`. `collectMarked` replaced two sorts of about 400,000 cells in the pack stage. Inner closures were slower at steady state (756 against 672 ms), so they are not used.

The coarse level far from the water is the mean of the near levels, as before. On the seven-falls course the water falls to about -1,613 m at the east end, so far cells read near -317 m. The bank treats ground past 3.5 m from the water as dry, so this changes nothing on screen.

**The renderer blends between pictures.** `createRiverWaterMaterial(..., previous)` mixes the previous and current flow textures with `uFlowBlend`, and the sheet moves each vertex from its `aPrevY` height to its current height. The scene copies each flow texture into its previous copy on the GPU before the new upload, and moves `uFlowBlend` from 0 to 1 over the mean time between pictures. The drawn water lags the newest picture by about one interval. The bank material is not blended yet.

## Progress discipline

1. A failed gate is evidence, not product progress by itself. Before the next progress checkpoint, execute a concrete repair or bounded causal diagnosis of its measured defect, unless a verified external wait or approval boundary prevents it. An unexecuted plan, tracker refresh or repeated status report does not satisfy this rule.
2. A runtime rejection stops promotion. When safe and useful, a separately labeled bounded offline diagnosis may continue far enough to test the required physical behavior; preserve the failed runtime gate. Do not repeatedly stop before impact and then imply that water behavior was tested.
3. An unavailable rendered view blocks visual acceptance, not independent source diagnosis, implementation or compute execution. Re-poll the same live handle; do not restart after a timeout. Mark the whole goal blocked only when the required consecutive-turn audit passes and no meaningful authorized work remains.
4. Every current action names the actual implementation, input/state, measured failure, next executable step and evidence that would prove improvement. Distinguish planned, built, running, terminal and verified. Check process/worker state before claiming activity. Current result and current next action govern; prior checkpoints are historical.
5. Consultations must be self-contained: supplied code/version, geometry, units, observed facts, measured limits and unknowns. Pro and Gemini cannot inspect local code or visuals. Use their answer for a concrete implementation decision and local test; avoid another generic recommendation or an endless code-audit ladder.
6. Make successful intermediate changes inspectable in the live or clearly labeled candidate scene, and judge motion over time. Preserve all original requirements and acceptance gates. Administrative work supports the water goal and does not replace it.

Pro distinguishes preserving positive water from preserving every nearly unsupported independent velocity mode. Geometry-aware aggregation may retain physical mass and momentum while reducing unreliable motion; its dissipation, connectivity and constraint behavior require measured checks. It is not permission to delete tiny water, join across air, invent support mass or relabel momentum errors as external forces. A disconnected droplet and an attached thin film require distinct physically meaningful representations.

The next acceptance event is ten physical seconds of a live inlet, crest, fall, impact, basin storage, secondary spill and outlet with continuous water rendering and full timing. It must then scale to the full-height scene. A better factorization of the old failing timestep is not the current work item. ## Lower-order candidate: first transport/contact failure

Verified: 2026-10-07 against the frozen source, worker reports, independent geometric moment integration and source/test review. This is failure evidence, not acceptance.

The fixed-cell RT0-like carrier integrates mass over convex wet cuts, including two-sided thin slabs. An independent 7 mm oblique slab control has volume 0.00405 m3; splitting it across 56 cells changes volume by -3.47e-18 m3 and matches analytic first and second moments. The moving update nevertheless applies a separate diagonal-affine characteristic map to each piece. Adjacent maps can overlap: donor-by-donor conservation does not supply a shared volume partition. Current wall constraints activate only on already-coincident faces; they do not yet handle approaching contact or departing inequality conditions. Axis-aligned source pieces also cannot develop oblique faces from diagonal maps alone.

The declared .005 s step stops at time zero on contact-rounding intersections. The 1/240 s diagnostic accepts one step and then stops on real liquid overlap. Its accepted-step volume residual is -1.90e-19 m3, momentum residual about 1e-16 kg m/s and divergence 5.58e-13 /s. Those quantities do not overrule the occupancy failure. Accepted-step CPU work is 8.51 ms for 4.17 ms of physical time. The report's full failed-run ratio includes diagnosis and is not a steady runtime measurement. No impact, storage, spill or refinement gate has passed.

The six tests are limited: hydrostatic projection checks rest and support impulse but no analytic pressure head; two disconnected boxes do not test the globally connected U with locally separated arms; the co-moving volume assertion lacks an absolute value and does not verify the expected translated shape. The pulse check tests arithmetic rather than integrated source-off behavior. Remap loss and centroid defect are initialized zeros because remap is not implemented, not measured successes. W07-W11 remain open.

Workflow improvement: require one short coupled contact/transport control immediately after the revised method, before another long sequence of isolated operator checks. Proposed control: source off, existing basin solid, h=.125 m, dt=1/240 s, gravity enabled, a patch from [1.9,.5025,2.875] to [2.15,.5275,3.125] moving at [.48,-.5,0] m/s, advance .03 s. Measure contact onset, wall impulse, actual occupancy, volume and physical momentum, and inspect redirection. Preserve the first failed state. Once it passes, return to the unchanged full ten-second cascade, refinement and rendered runtime gates. This is a proposed revised experiment pending method review, not a passed task.

The proposed source-off contact control was executed against the frozen candidate before any repair, to distinguish inlet defects from general contact. Its seed is valid and has volume 0.0015625 m3. The first 1/240 s step ends at minimum y=.5002463542. The second attempted step reaches y=.4978223958: 2.1776 mm inside the floor, with zero wall impulse and no liquid overlap. Solid intersection is 0.0001361003 m3, or 8.7104% of the seed. Independent constant-acceleration analysis places first contact at .0047762123 s, between the two steps, and independently reproduces the candidate's kick-drift position and overlap volume. This is a missing contact event, not just source rounding. Direct rejected-state volume and momentum closure remain near machine precision, again showing why closure alone does not establish physical behavior.

With solids removed, the same second step passes; the run then stops at accepted time .0208333 s, attempted .025 s, because one cell contains 35 cuts against the declared 32-cut limit. No overlap is measured. Controlled reconstruction is required even for this co-moving patch; increasing the limit alone would postpone the problem. Both outcomes and exact source hashes are in .agent/scratch/waterfall-gauntlet/cascade-contact-control/. Parent analytic review is cascade-contract/contact-independent-review.json. The candidate, tests and viewer were unchanged. The worker repeated each unchanged configuration once to enrich reporting, exceeding the literal two-execution cap; subsequent analysis used saved states without another run. Workflow improvement: save complete first-failure inputs, then derive added diagnostics from that saved state. No new implementation was accepted by that diagnostic. The exact private Pro request awaited approval at that point; the user approved it and submission was verified on 2026-10-08 as recorded below.

The live diagnostic viewer is .agent/scratch/waterfall-gauntlet/cascade-runtime-v1-view/live.html. The initial browser check exposed a stale Vite transform under the ignored scratch folder despite fresh files on disk. Fresh asset filenames and a client/worker identity handshake fix that mismatch. Parent browser review now shows build d2b0a6bd61f25ace, runtime 8120487c2fa1, dt=.005, matched worker and the actual stationary-solid rejection at time zero. The dry accepted geometry and failure are visible. This verifies diagnostic delivery, not waterfall appearance. Proof: cascade-contract/viewer-first-failure.png and viewer-first-failure-dom.txt. The existing native river and waterfall materials are outside this candidate.

Public research leads were checked independently while private Pro sharing awaited approval. [Basilisk geometric VOF](https://basilisk.fr/src/vof.h) uses shared face fluxes with directional compression terms and a CFL limit; its embedded-boundary approximation ignores solid volume in mixed cells, so it is not a drop-in match for this occupancy contract. [Han, Chiodi and Desjardins, 2024](https://arxiv.org/html/2403.10729v1) develops transported interface orientations and volume-constrained two-plane reconstruction for thin structures. [Tavares et al., 2024](https://arxiv.org/html/2402.10185v1) distinguishes solid velocity and contact-angle boundary conditions, but its subcell solid treatment has material limitations. These are method references for the next review, not proof that a combined browser implementation will pass. No private project payload was submitted to obtain these public sources.

Only the previously prepared 4,798-character request was sent; no additional private payload was added. It asks for a concrete shared conservative transport/contact/remap construction, recent primary research, an explicit numerical-tolerance assessment and one bounded implementation experiment. The request describes the source-step failures; the later inlet-free/capacity results remain local evidence for reviewing its advice. ### Completed shared-transport research

Verified: 2026-10-08 against the completed Pro response, primary papers and current candidate source. The answer is archived in ignored cascade-contract/pro-transport-completed.txt with its DOM and links. The research wait and sharing approval are resolved. This is a proposed implementation method; no physical or visual gate has passed from receiving advice.

Pro recommends one transient conforming partition of nearby wet and empty space, with shared faces, edges and vertices. One face owns one flux and one backtraced geometry. Positive donor intersections must supply both volume and physical momentum. Retain the low-order pressure candidate provisionally, strengthen actual oblique normal continuity, reconstruct thin material jointly inside disjoint receivers, and discard obsolete transport partitions each step. Empty extension is kinematic, owns no water mass and must not modify the physical wet field. Source input is one opening transaction; wall and liquid arrival require finite contact events. These additions are engineering adaptations, not guarantees supplied by the cited papers.

Primary-source checks:

- [Owkes and Desjardins, 2014](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jcp.2014.04.022): the authors' full paper on Cornell's site confirms common corner transport, simplex-based swept geometry and an interior correction point that matches the flux volume while preserving shared edges. The paper's Cartesian VOF construction is the starting point, not a proof for our locally separated cut carrier.
- [Remmerswaal and Veldman, 2022](https://arxiv.org/html/2209.14934v1): sections 3.2.1-3.2.4 distinguish overlap, gap, transit and flux-volume errors. Modified EMFPA retains unique remapped corners and corrects an interior face point. Its boundedness result has explicit donor assumptions; ordinary independent face shifts do not satisfy them. The 3D donating regions need not be convex.
- [Han, Chiodi and Desjardins, 2024](https://arxiv.org/html/2403.10729v1): transported surface data guides two-plane reconstruction and volume-constrained placement. Its thin-film example also reports centroid drift and thickening despite volume conservation. Our shape, centroid and energy checks therefore remain necessary; paired planes alone do not establish realism.
- [Huang and colleagues, revision 2 October 2026](https://arxiv.org/html/2606.02467v2): the current public revision and synchronized donor reconstruction are verified. The proposed method is directionally split and staggered, so reuse the consistency lesson, not a claim that this paper proves the proposed unsplit cut-cell adaptation.
- [Shewchuk's robust predicates](https://www.cs.cmu.edu/~quake/robust.html): reliable orientation signs address near-degenerate classification. They do not by themselves construct shared, exactly incident vertices. The floor discrepancy needs canonical constrained construction, not a larger overlap tolerance.

Parent interpretation: retain all W05 thresholds and the complete ten-second cascade as the useful acceptance event. Preserve native optics and the frozen failure states. The proposed backtraced receivers require actual positive decomposition, closure, capacity and non-folding checks; signed simplex bookkeeping must not be passed to the existing convex moment routine as positive material. One shared vertex is not by itself a conservative remap. Contact must use the same movement stage as transport and release at the finite rim. Reconstruct with current geometric evidence, not source labels or a shadow centroid ledger.

The source evidence supports parts of this direction, not the whole proposed coupling. [Han, Chiodi and Desjardins (2024)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2403.10729) reconstruct two interfaces locally from transported surface information and a volume-constrained solve, allowing films below the grid spacing. This does not establish arbitrary topology or browser performance. [Huang and colleagues, revised October 2, 2026](https://arxiv.org/html/2606.02467v2) identify momentum overshoots when momentum reconstruction does not match its mass donor; their synchronized-donor method and density-weighted time integration inform the transport contract. [Remmerswaal and Veldman](https://arxiv.org/html/2209.14934v1) distinguish donor overlap, gaps, transit and volume mismatch. Their transport analysis does not itself validate this project's pressure coupling.

One authoritative shared flux must move volume and momentum through the same donor region, with opposite entries for neighboring cells. The carrier is the integrated spline velocity through each face; a spline coefficient is not a uniform face speed. Reconstruct each local piece to its transported volume while retaining the discrepancy between its geometric centroid and transported first moment. Never conceal shape drift by overwriting that moment. After transport, apply pressure on the new physical geometry and update material momentum from that same field. Pressure momentum, hydrostatics and instantaneous divergence keep their existing gates; characteristic shape and finite-time motion need separate convergence checks.

The implementation sequence has five concrete gates: local geometry and pressure identities; a complete conservative moving step; separated/thin/contact regressions; a short crest/drop/basin/lower-spill chain running for several physical seconds; then total runtime cost and native exchange. Avoid another indefinite cube-test expansion. Start with simple walls and a roughly two-meter drop. A proposed 64 by 48 by 24 grid at 0.125-meter spacing is a workload to measure, not a performance prediction. The full-height waterfall and rapids remain the objective.

The first hydraulic chain may use a declared single-phase free surface with atmospheric traction. That can test takeoff, pressure-driven impact, pool storage, spill onset, source-off and flood arrival. It cannot establish entrained air, mist, aerodynamic breakup, capillary rivulets or the high waterfall's dispersed plume. Source and outlet exchange must debit and credit each volume/momentum packet once, replacing any scheduled injection for the same water. Preserve native optical ownership. Measure reconstruction, transport, pressure, memory and required arithmetic cost together; successful pressure timing alone cannot qualify live performance. Pro's full response is preserved in behavior-midpoint-review/pro-runtime-research.txt.
